10 THINGS TO EXPECT IN THE NFL TONIGHT:
TNF W9: JAX v BAL. 66°F, 60% Rain, 17 MPH Gusts.

1) The 5-2 Jacksonville Jaguars head into Baltimore to face The Flock, who continue to suffer injury setbacks to their multi-MVP QB in Lamar Jackson -- now in IR with a thumb injury. In the same game, their backup Tyler Huntley suffered a season ending toe injury. Woof.

While The Ravens recently traded for Cardinals backup Jacoby Brissett, he won't be starting for tonight's game; Instead, we get UConn product Joe Fagnano at the helm, who played the final 3 quarters of Week 7's blowout loss against The Bills.

2) To make matters worse for Fagnano, he'll be dealing with a solid chance for Rain (56%) and strong gusts (17 MPH) during the game. The Jaguars defense suffered two season ending injuries last Sunday, to DT Davon Hamilton (quad) and S Eric Murray (elbow).

Jesse Minter's Ravens have already been averse to passing, with a -4.2% Pass Rate over Expected (PROE), good for 24th in the league. Weather and a rookie QB doesn't necessarily provide Minter with the tools to stray from this rush dependency.

3) Before buying your Derrick Henry stock, let's talk about how incredible The Jags rush defense has been. They are currently posting Top 5 defensive rankings in:
- Success Rate (36.3%)
- OPP Rush TD (4)
- Explosive Rate (6.7%)
- Yds Before Contact (1.72)

Last one is notable, as Henry is sitting just 31st in Yds after Contact and well outside of The Top 50 in Explosive Rate. After rushing for 60+ yards in his first 5 games of the season, Henry has not surpassed that mark in any game since.

4) Fagnano threw 21 times in his season debut, with 4 going to Andrews (3 Rec) and another 4 going to Flowers -- none of which were completed, with one being intercepted. The Jaguars' secondary is running the 8th highest rate of zone coverage, while allowing the 6th highest rate of Yds/DB when doing so.

Their offense has been so strong, with a 52% average share of possession (7th best), that the Jags' coverage weaknesses have not translated to high opposing passing marks. Notable marks:
- Stroud 312 Yards, 24/34 C/A, 3 PTD
- Burrow 428 Yards, 39/54 C/A, 1 PTD
- Nix 288 Yards, 22/31 C/A, 1 PTD

5) Outside WRs have generated the 5th highest TGT/RR (targets per route ran) against Jacksonville, along with the 3rd highest Yds/RR; They have allowed the most yards to wide receivers on the season. Jakobi Lane has yet to run a route from anywhere but out wide, with Rashod Bateman typically being his outside partner.

Here are other receivers with >60% of routes ran out wide to face the Jaguars in their last 5 weeks (recent to past, min. 20 routes/gp):
- Keenan Allen 7 Rec, 67 Yds
- Nico Collins 3 Rec, 74 Yds
- Dontayvion Wicks 5 Rec, 63 Yds
- Darius Cooper 2 Rec, 71 Yds
- Tee Higgens 11 Rec, 151 Yds
- Dohnte Meyers 7 Rec, 82 Yds
- Mitch Tinsley 3 Rec, 49 Yds

Some productive history from this group. Ceiling is high for Lane and Bateman tonight if weather permits.

6) Bhayshul Tuten is questionable tonight, and was a DNP in all three practices this week -- not a great sign. In the previous 24 injury reports, there have been 27 instances where a player did not practice during the week. In all 27, the player missed the game that week (Stat via John Shipley).

Thus, we play into Chris Rodriguez Jr. as the top back for tonight, who was also limited all week but is not on the injury report here.

7) The Ravens are closer to a mid-pack rush defense, yet do have Top 10 rankings in STUFF (20.1%) and Explosive Rate (7.8%). There have been 6 running backs to log digit-double carries against Baltimore, and four of them logged 80+ rushing yards. Granted, this was a pretty talented group of running backs in Bijan, Taylor, Cook III, and Javonte Williams.

With Jags already dominating the time of possession battle, and Rodriguez's 4.6 YPC is elite enough to provide upside.

8) Over the past month, the Ravens have shown Cover 2 (2-HI) and Cover 3 (1-HI) in over half of their coverage looks. They have allowed the 4th most Air Yards in these two looks, yet are 11th in Yds/DB allowed as well.

Trevor Lawrence is amongst the premiere QBs in the league, yet sits 21st in Completion rate against those two specific looks amongst all QBs with >50 drop backs. However perspective is key here, as his 66.3% completion rate in this sample is actually beating his season average (65.7%) and any average of his career.

9) Brenton Strange is leading the Jags' pass-catcher room in 1st Read Share against Cover 2/3 at 25.2%. His matchup further improves as Tight Ends are producing the highest TPRR against Baltimore amongst all position groups at 0.21.

Here are TE1s against Baltimore, regardless of there specific coverage success:
- Kincaid 4 Rec, 86 Yds
- Gesicki 1 Rec, 6 Yds
- Fannin Jr. 1 Rec, 9 Yds
- Pitts Sr. 5 Rec, 42 Yds
- Gunnar Helm 1 Rec, 5 Yds

Yikes.

10) KICKERS and TRENDS!

Primetime favorites have now won three straight, moving them to 6-9 ATS on the year (only TNF & MNF). The Ravens come in here as 10 point dogs.

The Jaguars are allowing the 2nd fewest FGA/gp this season at just 1.4, which has improved further in their last 3 games to just 1 a game. Meanwhile, The Ravens are on the other end in this category, ranking 18th and facing a gung ho Cam Little.

With Ashton Jeanty likely reclaiming most of the backfield touches, I’m not expecting Washington to have much success in this matchup. The Raiders offense also ranks dead last in rushing success rate this season (32.4%).

HERE'S A RECAP OF WHAT PETER BECK AND HIS TEAM HAVE BEEN DOING.

Rocket Lab reports earnings on November 9 and I wanted to go through some of the developments we've seen during Q3 and since the quarter ended.

There's been a lot happening at  beyond Electron launches. Government contracts, satellite manufacturing, the Iridium acquisition, Neutron customers and new spacecraft technology.

1. $397M U.S. SPACE FORCE CONTRACT: AUGUST 4

Rocket Lab secured a contract worth up to $397M to develop, launch and operate Flatellite spacecraft for the Space Force's Space Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator program.

This is one of my favorite developments because Rocket Lab isn't simply providing a launch vehicle. It's taking responsibility for the satellites, their launch on Neutron and their operation in orbit.

It's a much bigger role in the defense supply chain.

2. $266M MISSILE DEFENSE CONTRACT — JULY 27

The Space Force awarded Rocket Lab a contract worth up to $266M for 12 suborbital launches, with options for six more.

These missions support missile defense testing and will primarily use the company's expanding launch infrastructure in Alaska.

It creates another source of launch demand outside traditional commercial satellite deployment.

3. 20 ADDITIONAL ELECTRON LAUNCHES FOR SYNSPECTIVE — SEPTEMBER 30

This was Rocket Lab's largest commercial Electron launch agreement to date.

Synspective signed for another 20 dedicated missions, bringing its total contracted Electron missions with Rocket Lab to 47.

Think about that customer relationship. Instead of booking one launch, evaluating another provider and repeating the process, Synspective continues expanding with Rocket Lab as its constellation grows.

4. THE IRIDIUM ACQUISITION MOVED CLOSER TO COMPLETION — SEPTEMBER

Rocket Lab completed a $1.944B at-the-market equity offering, issuing approximately 29.3M shares to help finance its proposed acquisition of Iridium.

It also arranged for Iridium's existing $1.775B term loan facility to remain in place after the transaction and terminated its $3.6B bridge financing commitment.

Yes, the equity raise created dilution. But the financing significantly reduces uncertainty around funding the acquisition.

The transaction still requires regulatory approvals and is expected to close in 2027.

If completed, Rocket Lab would move much further into owning and operating satellite communications services rather than just manufacturing and launching hardware.

5. EIGHT ROCKET LAB BUILT SATELLITE PLATFORMS REACHED ORBIT — AUGUST 16

Eight satellite platforms built by Rocket Lab for MDA Space successfully reached orbit to support Globalstar's constellation.

These are part of a $143M agreement covering 17 satellite platforms.

All eight established contact and were reported to be functioning normally.

This demonstrates something investors sometimes overlook. Rocket Lab is already a meaningful spacecraft manufacturer, even when another company is the prime contractor.

6. KEPLER BOOKED A DEDICATED NEUTRON LAUNCH — AUGUST 10

Kepler Communications selected Neutron to launch multiple satellites supporting optical connectivity, orbital computing and hosted payloads.

The mission is scheduled no earlier than 2028.

And this is worth watching because Rocket Lab is securing commercial launch commitments before Neutron enters service.

The demand is there. The engineering challenge is delivering the rocket.

7. ROCKET LAB ENTERED THE SPACE FORCE'S SPACE DATA NETWORK PROGRAM — AUGUST 18

Rocket Lab joined the Space Force's Space Data Network Consortium and received two delivery orders totaling $12M.

The work involves demonstrating interoperability for secure optical communications in space.

It may look small compared with the $397M contract, but it's another entry point into military communications infrastructure.

8. ROCKET LAB RELEASED ITS IMM APEX SOLAR CELL — SEPTEMBER 8

The new solar cell offers 31.5% beginning-of-life conversion efficiency and 40% lower mass.

It also eliminates the germanium substrate used in conventional multi junction solar cells.

I like this one because it shows how Rocket Lab is building a business around components that other spacecraft manufacturers need, not just the rockets carrying those spacecraft.

9. ELECTRON CONTINUED DELIVERING — THROUGH SEPTEMBER 30

Rocket Lab completed its 97th Electron flight in September, representing its 18th launch of 2026.

Then, after the quarter ended, it completed its 98th and 99th missions in October and November.

Launch reliability and repeatability are what make the commercial launch business viable.

Customers want their satellites delivered when promised.

10. NASA GDC TRAILBLAZER AWARD — OCTOBER 28

A federal contract record shows approximately $28.9M obligated to Rocket Lab for integration and flight of NASA's Geospace Dynamics Constellation Trailblazer payload.

The listed contract ceiling is approximately $36.8M, including options.

Another reminder that NASA remains an important customer across Rocket Lab's expanding launch portfolio.

11. NEUTRON'S FIRST FLIGHT MOVED TO 2027 — OCTOBER 14

We also need to discuss what didn't go according to plan.

Rocket Lab officially moved Neutron's first launch target from 2026 to 2027 following development and manufacturing challenges.

This is important because Neutron is central to several future contracts, including the Space Force Flatellite program.

The delay creates execution risk and I want management to provide a clearer timeline for qualification testing, development spending and the first flight.

There's no point ignoring this just because the company is winning contracts elsewhere.

NOW, WHAT WE SHOULD BE WATCHING ON MONDAY?

Rocket Lab previously guided for Q3 revenue of $250M–$265M, compared with the $234M it reported in Q2.

I'll be looking at revenue, gross margins, backlog, cash consumption, updated Neutron spending and how the company plans to integrate Iridium if the acquisition closes.

A few years ago, Rocket Lab was mostly discussed as a small rocket company competing for satellite launches.

Today, we're talking about a company manufacturing satellites, producing spacecraft components, developing medium lift rockets, securing hundreds of millions in defense contracts and potentially acquiring an established satellite communications operator.

It's a very different business. The important question is whether Rocket Lab can execute all these programs without allowing development costs, dilution and acquisition risks to overwhelm the economics.

The most imp part of Monday's earnings won't be just how many rockets Rocket Lab launched. It'll be how much progress the company has made toward becoming a fully integrated space infrastructure business.

Let's see what Peter Beck has to say.

here is how we made this video, 100% in code.

1. Storyboard (Figma) 6 frames showing every stage: guide lines, dimensions, outline, fill, details, final icon.

2. Design to code (Figma MCP + Claude Code) Claude exported each frame as SVG, then a script split the finished icon into 15 layers for separate animation.

3. Animating the drawing (Remotion + React + SVG) Each layer has its own moment on the timeline. Lines draw themselves like someone's drafting them. Labels type in letter by letter with a caret. The fill resolves out of fine dots.

4. The camera (CSS 3D) The icon sits on a tilted plane, camera looking at it low, oblique, macro. Shallow depth of field keeps only the action sharp. A pool of light follows the action, everything else fades to black.

5. The edit (Remotion) 9 shots, hard cuts, camera always drifting toward the next action. The finale travels over the icon, pulls back, lands front-on and centred.

6. Revisions (Claude Code + Chrome previews) Everything 28% faster. Wider frame, softer shadow, whole numbers only on dimensions. Last frame is pixel-sharp, grain fades out.

7. Sound (Python + NumPy) Music generated from the film's own timings. Every on-screen event has its own sound. Tempo rises with the edit from 100 to 138 BPM, ends on a hit and a chord.

8. Render (Remotion + ffmpeg) 1080p, 60fps, motion blur, AAC audio at 320kbps. 31 seconds. 4 minute render.
